title: Package managers: apt, dnf/yum and zypper

videos.script: Everything you have installed so far in this course arrived the same way, and you have not looked at it once. {{arrive}} A package manager is two things wearing one name. It is a database of what is on this machine and which file belongs to what — and it is a downloader that reads a list of what is available somewhere else. Almost every question you will have is one or the other, and knowing which halves the problem. {{two}} There are two families and you will meet both. Debian and Ubuntu use dot deb files, with apt on top and dpkg underneath. Red Hat, Rocky, Alma, Fedora and SUSE use dot rpm, with dnf or zypper on top and rpm underneath. The words differ and the ideas do not, which is why this lesson ends with a table you can read in either direction. {{families}} The part that costs people afternoons is dependencies. A package says what it needs, the manager works out the rest, and the failures are specific and recognisable — a package half installed, a file owned by nobody, a version held back on purpose by somebody who is no longer at the company. {{deps}} Every transcript here was run. The apt ones ran on this machine, which is Ubuntu. For the rpm side I built two small packages, put them in a repository, and installed them with dnf and with zypper — so the commands and their output are real even though the distribution is not. The section that uses them says so at the top. {{real}} {{title}}

This is the failure this lesson exists for, start to finish, and nothing in it is staged. {{open}} I download a package by hand — apt-get download cowsay — and install it with dpkg -i, which is what people do when they have a dot deb from somewhere. dpkg unpacks it and then stops: dependency problems prevent configuration. It needs a perl module that is not here. {{dpkg}} Now look at the state. dpkg -l shows i-U, which is a letter pair worth learning: the first says somebody wanted it installed, the second says it is unpacked and not configured. It is half in. {{state}} And half in is not a theoretical problem. Running cowsay gets a perl error about a missing module, four lines long, that names no package at all. If you had met this error without having done the install yourself, you would have no idea it was a packaging problem. {{error}} The repair is one command. apt-get --fix-broken install reads the dependency dpkg could not satisfy, fetches it, and then finishes configuring the package that was waiting. Two lines of output and it is over. {{fix}} That is the shape of the whole lesson: dpkg and rpm do one package and do what they are told. apt and dnf know what else is needed. Reach for the low-level one and you own the consequences — which is fine, as long as you know the command that hands them back. {{close}}

Three things worth keeping from this lesson. {{three}} The first is that the package manager knows. Which file belongs to what, what is installed, what a package would pull in, why a version is the one you got — all of it is a query away, and people guess at it instead. dpkg -S on a file you are unsure about costs nothing. {{knows}} The second is that a file in slash usr slash local belongs to nobody, and that is the point of it. Lesson three said that directory is for things you installed yourself; this lesson is why it is a separate directory. The package manager will not touch it and cannot help you with it. {{local}} And the third is that everything you add outside the distribution's repositories is yours to maintain. A third-party repository, a pip install, a binary from a release page — each one is a thing that will not be upgraded when the machine is, and will not be mentioned when it is the reason something broke. {{outside}} Next is text: grep, sed, awk, and the pipes that join them. It is the lesson that turns the terminal from a place you run commands into a place you answer questions. {{next}}
